terms.standardEnglish: These are the sons of Jacob, that were born to him in Paddan-aram (ASV); these are Jacob's sons, who were born to him in Paddan-aram (NJPS); these were the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram (NRSV)
terms.wohChoice: These are the sons of Ya'aqov, who were born to him in Paddan-Aram (ASV-baseline with WoH transliteration)
terms.rationale:
**Gen 35:26's closing formula *eleh b-nei Ya'aqov asher yullad-lo b-Paddan-Aram* — *these are the sons of Ya'aqov who were born to him in Paddan-Aram* — contradicts the chapter's own vv 16-18: Binyamin, named in the Rachel-list at v 24, was born between Beit-El and Efrat in Kena'an (vv 16-18), not in Paddan-Aram.** The contradiction is one of Genesis's clearest documentary-seams and is editorially-unresolved at the surface-narrative level.

**(a) The contradiction in detail.** The chapter's narrative-sequence:

- **vv 1-15** — the return to Beit-El, the second renaming, the El Shaddai covenant-promise, the matzevah-and-libation installation.
- **vv 16-18** — the journey from Beit-El toward Efrat, Rachel's labor and death, Binyamin's birth *kivrat ha-aretz* (*some distance*) from Efrat — explicitly *in the land*, not in Paddan-Aram.
- **vv 19-20** — Rachel's burial *b-derekh Efratah hi Beit-Lechem* (*on the way to Efrat, that is Beit-Lechem*); the burial matzevah.
- **vv 21-22** — Yisra'el's journey beyond Migdal-Eder; Re'uven's deed.
- **vv 22b-26** — the formal-genealogical-list of the twelve sons, organized by mother (Le'ah, Rachel, Bilhah, Zilpah), with the closing formula *eleh b-nei Ya'aqov asher yullad-lo b-Paddan-Aram*.
- **vv 27-29** — Ya'aqov's arrival at Hevron; Yitzchaq's death.

Binyamin is named in v 24 in the Rachel-list (*b-nei Rachel Yosef u-Vinyamin*) and in v 26 in the closing formula (*eleh b-nei Ya'aqov asher yullad-lo b-Paddan-Aram*). The formal-genealogical-list at vv 22b-26 includes Binyamin as one of the twelve sons born in Paddan-Aram. But vv 16-18 of the same chapter narrate Binyamin's birth in Kena'an. The contradiction is internal to the chapter — the same chapter that narrates Binyamin's Kena'an-birth also lists Binyamin among the sons born in Paddan-Aram.

**(b) The modern critical documentary-source analysis.** Modern critical scholarship reads v 26 as a P-redactional genealogical-list-fragment harmonized imperfectly with the older J/E Binyamin-birth-narrative:

- **Speiser** *AB Genesis* 1964 pp. 274-275 — *the formal list ... overlooks the fact ... that Binyamin was born in Kena'an. The discrepancy is a clear sign that the list is a separate-source-fragment integrated without full-harmonization*.
- **Westermann** *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 558-559 — treats v 26 as a P-source genealogical-list that has been editorially-juxtaposed with the J/E Binyamin-birth-narrative without harmonization; the redactor accepted the contradiction rather than smoothing it.
- **Hamilton** *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 379-381 — preserves the source-critical reading and notes that the redactor's preservation of the contradiction is itself editorially-significant; the discrepancy is a *fossilized* source-seam.
- **Skinner** *ICC Genesis* 1910 pp. 426-427 — identifies v 26 as P and notes the contradiction explicitly as a documentary-marker.
- **Friedman** *The Bible with Sources Revealed* 2003 — assigns vv 22b-26 (the genealogical-list) to P and vv 16-20 (the Binyamin-birth-narrative) to E; the contradiction is the source-seam between the two.
- **Carr** *Reading the Fractures of Genesis* 1996 — uses Gen 35:26 as an exemplar-case for the documentary-source-criticism method.

The contradiction is therefore one of Genesis's clearest documentary-source-seams. The mainstream modern-critical consensus is that v 26 reflects an older P-source tradition in which all twelve sons (including Binyamin) were born in Paddan-Aram, and the redactor of Genesis integrated this list with the J/E Kena'an-birth-narrative without resolving the temporal-and-geographical contradiction.

**(c) The traditional / harmonizing readings.** Pre-modern Jewish-and-Christian commentary attempted various harmonizations:

- **Rashi** at Gen 35:26 — *all of them were born in Paddan-Aram except Binyamin; nevertheless, since most were born in Paddan-Aram, the formula speaks generally*. The *majority-principle* (*hatlinan b-zol*) harmonization.
- **Ibn Ezra** at Gen 35:26 — preserves the Rashi-harmonization with additional grammatical analysis.
- **Ramban** (Nachmanides) at Gen 35:26 — similar majority-principle harmonization with additional theological-reflection on the editorial-deliberateness.
- **Calvin** *Commentaries on Genesis* — adopts the majority-principle and notes the *generally-speaking* register.

The traditional harmonizations preserve the canonical-coherence but at the cost of accepting that the formula's *kol* (all) carries an implicit *most* qualifier. Modern critical scholarship rejects this harmonization as ad-hoc and reads the contradiction as documentary.

**(d) The P-source genealogical-list tradition.** The P-source's distinctive genealogical-list-formulae recur throughout Genesis: the *toldot* formulae (Gen 5, 10, 11, 25:12-18, 36); the formal-list pattern of organized-by-mother / organized-by-tribal-ancestor; the *asher yullad-lo* (who-was-born-to-him) formula. The Gen 35:22b-26 list shares these markers and fits the P-source profile.

Modern critical scholarship reads the P-source as having its own twelve-tribe-tradition in which the tribal-eponyms were all born in Paddan-Aram, possibly reflecting a tradition that the patriarchal-period was schematized as fully-Aramean before the return to Kena'an. The J/E-tradition (Gen 35:16-20) preserved a more-detailed Binyamin-birth-narrative that placed the birth in Kena'an. The two traditions were combined by the redactor without harmonization, leaving the v 26 *all in Paddan-Aram* formula in contradiction with the v 16-18 *Binyamin in Kena'an* narrative.

**(e) The chronological-side of the contradiction.** The contradiction also has a chronological dimension: Rachel dies giving birth to Binyamin (v 18). If Binyamin was born in Paddan-Aram (per v 26), Rachel would have died in Paddan-Aram, but Gen 31:14-16 has Rachel alive throughout Paddan-Aram and Gen 31:17-21 narrates the family's departure from Paddan-Aram with Rachel still alive. The chronological-coherence requires Binyamin's birth and Rachel's death to occur in Kena'an (consistent with vv 16-20), not in Paddan-Aram (inconsistent with v 26). The contradiction is therefore both geographical and chronological.

**(f) Translation choice.** The WoH renders *These are the sons of Ya'aqov, who were born to him in Paddan-Aram* (ASV-baseline with WoH transliteration). The verse is rendered as the MT presents it, with the contradiction preserved unresolved. The commentary documents the documentary-seam observation. The translation does not soften the *all* to *most* or otherwise smooth the contradiction.

**(g) Why overlay, not central.** The contradiction is chapter-specific: it is internal to Gen 35 (between vv 16-18 and v 26). The P-source genealogical-list tradition has wider HB cross-corpus reach (the *toldot* formulae across Genesis), but the specific Paddan-Aram / Binyamin contradiction is chapter-singular. The entry is housed in the overlay per the ratified architectural-split.

**Modern scholarly literature.** Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 245-246; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 558-559; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* 1994 p. 327; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 379-381; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 pp. 274-275; Skinner *ICC Genesis* 1910 pp. 426-427; Friedman *The Bible with Sources Revealed* 2003; Carr *Reading the Fractures of Genesis* 1996; Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 199; Rashi at Gen 35:26; Ibn Ezra at Gen 35:26; Ramban at Gen 35:26; for the documentary-source-criticism method generally: Whybray *The Making of the Pentateuch* 1987; Ska *Introduction to Reading the Pentateuch* 2006; Nicholson *The Pentateuch in the Twentieth Century* 1998.

The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the contradiction is HB-internal-explicit (vv 16-18 vs v 26); (b) the modern critical documentary-source-analysis (Speiser, Westermann, Skinner, Hamilton, Friedman, Carr) is mainstream; (c) the chronological-dimension of the contradiction is verifiable by reading the Gen 31 departure-narrative against the Gen 35:16-18 birth-narrative; (d) the traditional harmonizations (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Ramban) are documented and represent the pre-modern attempts to resolve the contradiction; (e) the editorial-preservation of the contradiction by the redactor is mainstream modern-critical scholarship.

terms.partOfSpeech: compound place-name identification (three proper-names linked by *hi* — *the same is*)
terms.literal: Mamre, Qiryat-Arba — the same is Hevron
terms.standardEnglish: Mamre, to Kirjath-arba (the same is Hebron) (ASV); Mamre, at Kiriath-arba — that is Hebron (NJPS); Mamre, or Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) (NRSV)
terms.wohChoice: Mamre, to Qiryat-Arba (the same is Hevron) (ASV-baseline-structure with WoH transliteration for all three names)
terms.rationale:
**Gen 35:27's *va-yavo Ya'aqov el-Yitzchaq aviv Mamre Qiryat-ha-Arba hi Hevron asher gar sham Avraham v-Yitzchaq* — *and Ya'aqov came to Yitzchaq his father at Mamre, to Qiryat-Arba — the same is Hevron — where Avraham and Yitzchaq sojourned* — deploys the chapter-distinctive triple-toponym identification of the patriarchal-encampment site at Hevron.**

**(a) The three toponyms.**

*(i) Mamre* (מַמְרֵא) — the patriarchal-encampment-locale, named for an Amorite confederate of Avraham (Gen 14:13, 24). The toponym recurs across the patriarchal narratives:
- **Gen 13:18** (Avraham's altar at the *elonei Mamre*).
- **Gen 14:13, 24** (Mamre the Amorite and his brothers Eshkol and Aner as Avraham's confederates in the Kdorla'omer war).
- **Gen 18:1** (the three-visitors-theophany at the *elonei Mamre*).
- **Gen 23:17, 19** (the Makhpelah-cave purchase: the cave *al-pnei Mamre*).
- **Gen 25:9** (Avraham's burial *al-pnei Mamre*).
- **Gen 35:27** (here).
- **Gen 49:30; 50:13** (Ya'aqov's burial-instructions referencing *Mamre*).

The toponym is consistently associated with the Hevron-area patriarchal-encampment and with the *elonei Mamre* — the *oaks (or terebinths) of Mamre* — a tree-cultic-site (see central [elonei-mamre](#elonei-mamre)).

*(ii) Qiryat-Arba* (קִרְיַת הָאַרְבַּע) — the pre-Israelite-period toponym of Hevron, literally *city of four* or *city of Arba*. The dual-etymology:
- **Josh 14:15** — *v-shem Hevron l-fanim Qiryat-Arba ha-adam ha-gadol ba-Anaqim hu* — *and the name of Hevron formerly was Qiryat-Arba; this Arba was the greatest man among the Anaqim*. The Joshua-verse provides an in-text-etymology: Qiryat-Arba is named for *Arba*, an Anaqim hero. The Anaqim-tradition is preserved at Num 13:22, 28, 33 (Anaqim as one of the giant-classes); Deut 1:28; 2:10-11; 9:2 (the Anaqim as the *Refa'im*-class).
- **Josh 15:13, 54; 20:7; 21:11; Judg 1:10; Neh 11:25** — the toponym recurs in tribal-allocation, judges-period, and post-exilic contexts.

The alternative etymology *city of four* (taking *Arba* as the numeral *four*) suggests a four-quarters or four-tribes city-structure. The two etymologies are not mutually-exclusive: Hevron may have been called *Qiryat-Arba* originally for one reason (the Anaqim-hero Arba) with a folk-etymological reinterpretation (city of four) developing later.

*(iii) Hevron* (חֶבְרוֹן) — the standard-Israelite-period name. The toponym derives from the root *ch-v-r* (associate, join) — *the place of association*. Hevron is one of the foundational patriarchal-and-Davidic cities: David is anointed king there (2 Sam 2:1-4, 5:1-5) and reigns there for seven-and-a-half years before moving the capital to Jerusalem. The post-exilic period preserves the Hevron-name; the modern Arabic *al-Khalil* (the *friend*) renames the city for Avraham as the *friend of Allah* (cf. Isa 41:8 *Avraham ohavi* — *Avraham my friend*; the Christian-and-Islamic *Abraham the Friend* tradition).

**(b) The triple-toponym pattern.** The Gen 35:27 verse uses the *hi* (the-same-is) construction to link the three toponyms into a single-place-identification. The pattern is editorially-deliberate and recurs across the HB at:
- **Gen 23:2** (Sarah's death-narrative): *va-tamot Sarah b-Qiryat-Arba hi Hevron b-eretz Kena'an* — *and Sarah died in Qiryat-Arba, the same is Hevron, in the land of Kena'an*.
- **Gen 23:19** (the Makhpelah-cave purchase): *me-arat sdeh ha-Makhpelah al-pnei Mamre hi Hevron* — *the cave of the field of the Makhpelah before Mamre, the same is Hevron*.
- **Gen 35:27** (here).
- **Josh 14:15** (the conquest-allocation): *v-shem Hevron l-fanim Qiryat-Arba* — *and the name of Hevron formerly was Qiryat-Arba*.
- **Josh 20:7** (the cities-of-refuge): *et-Qiryat-Arba hi Hevron b-har Yehudah* — *Qiryat-Arba, the same is Hevron, in the hill-country of Yehudah*.

The pattern's editorial-function is to bridge the pre-Israelite and Israelite naming-traditions: the older name (*Qiryat-Arba*) is acknowledged alongside the standard-Israelite-name (*Hevron*), with *Mamre* preserved as the patriarchal-encampment-locale. The triple-identification preserves continuity across naming-traditions.

**(c) The Makhpelah-cave-burial-site connection.** The site contains the Makhpelah-cave-burial-complex: Sarah's burial (Gen 23, the inaugural patriarchal-acquisition of land in Kena'an); Avraham's burial (Gen 25:9); Yitzchaq's and Rivkah's burial (Gen 49:31, Ya'aqov's deathbed inventory); Le'ah's burial (Gen 49:31); Ya'aqov's burial (Gen 50:13). The five-burial-chain is the foundational-tradition of the patriarchal-Hevron-tomb (see central [me-arat-ha-makhpelah-cave-etymology-hebron-tomb](#me-arat-ha-makhpelah-cave-etymology-hebron-tomb)). The Gen 35:27 *Mamre Qiryat-Arba hi Hevron* identification is editorially-significant because it anchors the entire burial-chain at the named-site immediately before the patriarchal-generation-arc closes with Yitzchaq's death and burial (vv 28-29).

**(d) The Davidic-and-post-exilic reception.** Hevron is the foundational-Davidic city: David is anointed king-of-Yehudah at Hevron (2 Sam 2:1-4) and king-over-all-Yisra'el at Hevron (2 Sam 5:1-5). The post-exilic period preserves the patriarchal-Hevron tradition: Neh 11:25 records the post-exilic restoration of Hevron / Qiryat-Arba as a Yehudite settlement. The Herodian-period enclosure-walls at the Makhpelah-cave-tomb (the *al-Haram al-Ibrahimi* / *Cave of the Patriarchs*) are the largest Herodian-construction outside Jerusalem and preserve the 1st-century-BCE identification of the site as the patriarchal-tomb (Josephus *Antiquities* I.237; *Jewish War* IV.532).

**(e) Translation choice.** The WoH renders *Mamre, to Qiryat-Arba (the same is Hevron)* (ASV-baseline-structure with WoH transliteration for all three names). The ASV exact *Mamre, to Kirjath-arba* uses an older-transliteration of *Qiryat-Arba*; the WoH choice modernizes to *Qiryat-Arba* with the *q* representing the *qoph* and the *kh* (not present here) maintained as the standard transliteration. *Hevron* (rather than ASV *Hebron*) preserves the *v*-spirant. The parenthetical *the same is Hevron* preserves the *hi*-construction.

**(f) Why overlay, not central.** The triple-toponym identification recurs across multiple HB verses (Gen 23:2, 19; 35:27; Josh 14:15; 20:7); the cross-corpus reach is substantial. However, each of the three constituent-toponyms (*Mamre*, *Qiryat-Arba*, *Hevron*) is already covered or could be covered by individual central-glossary entries; the *Makhpelah-cave-burial-site* is covered by the existing [me-arat-ha-makhpelah-cave-etymology-hebron-tomb](#me-arat-ha-makhpelah-cave-etymology-hebron-tomb) central entry. The specific *triple-toponym-identification* pattern is chapter-specific in its Gen 35:27 deployment (the verse explicitly links all three names with two *hi*-constructions), and the entry is housed in the overlay per the ratified architectural-split. The cross-corpus extension may justify promotion to central in a future revision if the triple-identification pattern recurs across additional verses requiring central treatment.

**Modern scholarly literature.** Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 246; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 560-561; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* 1994 p. 328; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 381; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 274; Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 199; for Hevron-archaeology: A. Ofer *Hebron* in *NEAEHL* 1993 vol. 2 pp. 606-609; for the Anaqim-tradition: Stuart *Hosea-Jonah* WBC 1987 (on Hos 9:13 Anaqim-reference); for the Davidic-Hevron: McCarter *II Samuel* AB 1984 pp. 87-89; HALOT s.v. *Mamre*, *Qiryat-Arba*, *Hevron*; BDB pp. 577, 900, 289.

The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the triple-toponym identification at Gen 35:27 is grammatically explicit; (b) the cross-corpus distribution of the pattern at Gen 23:2, 19; Josh 14:15; 20:7 is verifiable by lexical search; (c) the Anaqim / four-quarters etymology-pair for *Qiryat-Arba* is documented in Josh 14:15; (d) the Makhpelah-burial-chain is HB-internal-explicit and is covered by the existing central entry; (e) the Davidic-and-post-exilic reception is documentary; (f) the Herodian-period archaeological evidence for the patriarchal-tomb identification is documented in Josephus.

terms.partOfSpeech: verb (vav-consec qal 3ms of *halakh*) + proper-name + waw-conjunct + verb (vav-consec qal 3ms of *shakhav*) + accusative-marker + proper-name + noun (pilegesh) + noun with 3ms suffix
terms.literal: and Re'uven went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine
terms.standardEnglish: Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine (ASV/NRSV); Reuben went and lay with his father's concubine Bilhah (NJPS)
terms.wohChoice: Re'uven went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine (ASV-baseline-structure with WoH transliteration of *Re'uven*; the succession-claim ANE-typology and the Gen 49:3-4 retrospective preserved in commentary and in this glossary entry)
terms.rationale:
**Gen 35:22's *va-yelekh Re'uven va-yishkav et-Bilhah pilegesh aviv va-yishma Yisra'el* — *and Re'uven went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine, and Yisra'el heard* — is one of the chapter's most editorially-load-bearing interpretive cruxes.** The verse poses three integrated questions: (a) the nature of the deed (literal sexual offense or symbolic succession-claim); (b) the patriarchal-response (Ya'aqov's silence in Gen 35; the explicit deathbed-curse at Gen 49:3-4); (c) the ANE-comparative succession-claim typology.

**(a) The literal-vs-symbolic reading.** Modern critical scholarship reads the deed as either (i) literal incest with the father's-concubine, in violation of the later-codified Lev 18:8 / 20:11 / Deut 22:30 [MT 23:1] step-mother taboo; or (ii) symbolic succession-claim, in which the firstborn appropriates the father's-bed-and-concubine to claim primacy and to displace the patriarch from his position. The two readings are not mutually-exclusive: the deed may have been simultaneously a literal sexual-encounter and a politically-motivated succession-claim. The mainstream modern critical reading emphasizes the succession-claim dimension.

Key scholarship:
- **Sarna** *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 244 — *the deed is a political move; by taking his father's concubine Re'uven asserts his claim to leadership of the clan*. Sarna preserves both the literal-and-symbolic dimensions but emphasizes the succession-claim reading.
- **Westermann** *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 558-559 — preserves the symbolic-succession-claim reading and treats the deed within the ANE-comparative pattern.
- **Hamilton** *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 380-381 — preserves both readings; treats the deed's reception in Gen 49:3-4 as confirming the political-significance.
- **Speiser** *AB Genesis* 1964 pp. 273-274 — emphasizes the succession-claim reading with ANE-comparative material.
- **Alter** *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 198-199 — preserves the literal-and-symbolic-tension; reads the Gen 49:3-4 deathbed-curse as the retrospective-judgment that confirms the political-dimension.
- **Friedman** *The Bible with Sources Revealed* 2003 — assigns the deed-narration to E with possible J residue; the source-critical analysis treats the deed as preserved-from-an-older-tradition.

**(b) The Gen 49:3-4 retrospective curse.** Ya'aqov's deathbed-blessing-and-curse at Gen 49:3-4 explicitly cites the deed and pronounces judgment on Re'uven:

*Re'uven b'khori atah kochi v-reshit oni yeter s'et v-yeter az pachaz ka-mayim al-totar ki alita mishkevei avikha az chillalta yetzu'i alah*

*Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the first of my vigor; the excellency of dignity and the excellency of power. Unstable as water, you shall not have the preeminence, because you went up to your father's bed; then you defiled it — he went up to my couch.*

The curse confirms:
*(i)* the deed's editorial-significance — the patriarchal-deathbed-curse explicitly cites *mishkevei avikha* (*your father's bed*) and *yetzu'i alah* (*he went up to my couch*);
*(ii)* the loss-of-firstborn-status — *pachaz ka-mayim al-totar* (*unstable as water, you shall not have the preeminence*); Re'uven loses the firstborn-status that the introductory *b'khori atah kochi v-reshit oni* affirms;
*(iii)* the succession-claim reading — the firstborn-status loss is the patriarchal-response to the succession-claim attempt; by claiming primacy through the father's-bed, Re'uven forfeits the primacy he held by birth-order.

The 1 Chr 5:1-2 reception confirms: *u-v-hallo yetzu'ei aviv nittnah b'khorato li-vnei Yosef ben-Yisra'el v-lo l-hityaches la-b'khorah* — *when he defiled his father's couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Yosef son of Yisra'el, and he is not to be reckoned in the genealogy according to the birthright*. The Chronicler's reception explicitly transfers the firstborn-status from Re'uven to Yosef (in the form of Ephrayim-and-Menasheh as the double-portion-inheritance recipients) on the basis of the Gen 35:22 deed.

**(c) The ANE-comparative succession-claim typology.** The deed fits an ANE pattern of *succession-claim-by-bed*: the appropriation of the senior-male's wife-or-concubine as a political-claim to his position. The HB-internal parallels:

- **2 Sam 16:21-22** (Avshalom takes David's concubines): *va-yomer Achitofel el-Avshalom bo el-pilagshei avikha asher hinniach li-shmor ha-bayit v-shama kol-Yisra'el ki niv'ashta et-avikha v-chazqu y'dei kol-asher itakh* — *and Achitofel said to Avshalom: Go in to your father's concubines, whom he has left to keep the house; and all Yisra'el will hear that you have made yourself odious to your father; then will the hands of all who are with you be strengthened*. Avshalom then *va-yet l-Avshalom ha-ohel al-ha-gag va-yavo Avshalom el-pilagshei aviv l-eynei kol-Yisra'el* — *they spread a tent for Avshalom on the roof, and Avshalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Yisra'el*. The political-significance is explicit: Achitofel advises this as the most-decisive succession-claim possible.
- **1 Kgs 2:13-25** (Adoniyah's request for Avishag the Shunemmite): Adoniyah, after losing the succession-struggle to Shlomo, requests through Bat-Sheva the hand of Avishag the Shunemmite — David's last-attending-companion-or-concubine. Shlomo recognizes the request as an implicit-succession-claim and executes Adoniyah: *v-shavti ata l-shol et-Avishag ha-Shunamit l-Adoniyah u-sho-l-li et-ha-malkhut ki hu achi ha-gadol mimenni v-lo u-l-Evyatar ha-kohen u-l-Yo'av ben-Tzeruyah* — *you might as well ask the kingdom for him too, for he is my elder brother*. The political-equivalence of *taking the king's concubine* and *taking the kingdom* is explicit in Shlomo's response.
- **2 Sam 3:7** (Avner and Sha'ul's concubine Rizpah): Ish-Bosheth challenges Avner for taking Rizpah, Sha'ul's concubine. The challenge is read as Ish-Bosheth recognizing Avner's implicit-succession-claim; Avner responds with offense and defects to David. The pattern is consistent: taking the senior-male's concubine is read as a succession-claim, with political-consequences.

**(d) The ANE legal-comparative material.** Multiple ANE legal-codes preserve prohibitions on the seduction-of-the-father's-concubine or wife:

- **The Hittite Laws** (HL §195) — prohibits sexual-relations between a son and his father's wife as a capital-offense.
- **The Middle Assyrian Laws** (MAL §41) — regulates the secondary-wife status and prohibits unauthorized relations with the father's secondary-wife.
- **The Hammurabi Code** (CH §157) — prohibits sexual-relations between a son and his mother (after the father's death); the punishment is execution-by-burning.
- **Deut 22:30 [MT 23:1]** (the HB step-mother-taboo): *lo yiqach ish et-eshet aviv v-lo y'galeh k'naf aviv* — *a man shall not take his father's wife, nor uncover his father's skirt*.
- **Lev 18:8** (the holiness-code prohibition): *ervat eshet avikha lo t'galleh ervat avikha hi* — *the nakedness of your father's wife you shall not uncover; it is your father's nakedness*.
- **Lev 20:11** (the punishment): *v-ish asher yishkav et-eshet aviv ervat aviv gillah mot yumtu shneihem dmeihem bam* — *a man who lies with his father's wife has uncovered his father's nakedness; both of them shall be put to death; their blood is upon them*.

The HB step-mother-taboo at Lev 18:8, 20:11 and Deut 22:30 codifies the prohibition that the Gen 35:22 deed violates. The Gen 49:3-4 deathbed-curse is the patriarchal-response that the later legal-codification preserves as a capital-offense; the difference between the patriarchal-response (curse, loss of firstborn-status) and the Mosaic-response (execution) reflects the legal-development between the patriarchal-period and the codified-Israelite-law.

**Key ANE-comparative scholarship.** **Westbrook** *Studies in Ancient Near Eastern Family Law* 1988 and *Property and the Family in Biblical Law* JSOTSup 113 (1991); **Tigay** *Deuteronomy* AB 1996 (on the step-mother-taboo and the ANE-comparative material); **van Seters** *Abraham in History and Tradition* 1975 (on succession-claims in patriarchal narratives); **Roth** *Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor* 1995 (the standard ANE legal-code anthology).

**(e) The patriarchal-silence at v 22.** *Va-yishma Yisra'el* (*and Yisra'el heard*) marks Ya'aqov's reception of the news but no narrative-response. The patriarchal-silence is editorially-deliberate: the response is deferred to the deathbed-curse at Gen 49:3-4. The deferral has been read by modern critical scholarship as:
*(i)* preserving the patriarch's dignity at the immediate-moment (Ya'aqov does not act in anger);
*(ii)* setting up the deathbed-curse as the formal-judgment with appropriate solemnity;
*(iii)* reflecting the editorial-structure in which patriarchal-judgments are delivered at deathbed-blessings (Gen 27 for Yitzchaq's blessing; Gen 49 for Ya'aqov's; the deathbed-blessing as the canonical-locus for patriarchal-judgment).

The *piska b-emtza pasuq* (paragraph-break in the middle of the verse) marker between *va-yishma Yisra'el* and *va-yihyu b-nei Ya'aqov shneim asar* is editorially-deliberate: the break marks the gravity-of-the-moment and the patriarchal-silence (see central [piska-b-emtza-pasuq-masoretic-paragraph-break](#piska-b-emtza-pasuq-masoretic-paragraph-break)).

**(f) The *pilegesh* status-class.** Bilhah's named-status here as *pilegesh aviv* (his-father's-concubine) is editorially-significant: she has been previously named as *shifchah* (handmaid, Gen 29:29; 30:3-8). The status-shift from *shifchah* to *pilegesh* parallels Hagar's status-shift across the Avraham-cycle. The lexeme *pilegesh* is covered in the central [pilegesh-concubine-status-class](#pilegesh-concubine-status-class) entry.

**(g) Translation choice.** The WoH renders *Re'uven went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine* (ASV-baseline-structure with WoH transliteration of *Re'uven*). The verb-cluster *halakh*-and-*shakhav* preserves the deliberate sequence of action (he went, he lay-with); the lexeme *pilegesh* is rendered *concubine* per the central glossary entry. The deed is rendered as the MT presents it, without softening or expanding; the interpretive-tradition (literal-vs-symbolic, succession-claim, retrospective-curse) is documented in commentary and in this glossary entry.

**(h) Lens-discipline.** The symbolic-succession-claim reading is mainstream modern critical scholarship (Sarna, Westermann, Hamilton, Speiser, Alter, Westbrook, Tigay, van Seters) — it is *not* WoH-distinctive synthesis. The HB-internal parallels (2 Sam 16:21-22, 1 Kgs 2:13-25, 2 Sam 3:7) and the ANE-comparative material (HL, MAL, CH) provide the documentary-support. Any project-specific synthesis (a WoH-distinctive reading of the deed's wider significance within the patriarchal-narrative's broader frame) is reserved for the wiki and is not preempted by this entry.

**(i) Why overlay, not central.** The deed is chapter-specific to Gen 35:22 with its Gen 49:3-4 retrospective. The *pilegesh* status-class lexeme is housed in the central glossary (it has wide cross-corpus distribution); the *piska b-emtza pasuq* phenomenon is also housed centrally (it has wide cross-corpus distribution as a Masoretic-textual phenomenon). This overlay entry covers only the chapter-specific Re'uven-Bilhah deed and its Gen 49:3-4 retrospective — the integrated-interpretive crux that is chapter-singular. The three-entry split (central *pilegesh*, central *piska*, overlay Re'uven-Bilhah deed) preserves the architectural-discipline: cross-corpus lexica and phenomena are central; chapter-specific interpretive cruxes are overlay.

**Modern scholarly literature.** Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 244; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 558-559; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* 1994 pp. 327-328; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 380-381; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 pp. 273-274; Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 198-199; Skinner *ICC Genesis* 1910 pp. 426-427; Friedman *The Bible with Sources Revealed* 2003; Westbrook *Studies in Ancient Near Eastern Family Law* 1988; Westbrook *Property and the Family in Biblical Law* JSOTSup 113 (1991); Tigay *Deuteronomy* AB 1996; van Seters *Abraham in History and Tradition* 1975; Roth *Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor* 1995; on the 2 Sam 16 / 1 Kgs 2 parallels: McCarter *II Samuel* AB 1984; DeVries *I Kings* WBC 1985; for rabbinic-reception: b. Shabbat 55b (Rabbi Yonatan's defense of Re'uven); Genesis Rabbah 82:11; Rashi at Gen 35:22.

The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the deed-narration at Gen 35:22 is grammatically explicit; (b) the Gen 49:3-4 deathbed-curse explicitly cites the deed (*alita mishkevei avikha az chillalta yetzu'i alah*); (c) the 1 Chr 5:1-2 reception is HB-internal-explicit; (d) the HB-internal parallels at 2 Sam 16:21-22, 1 Kgs 2:13-25, 2 Sam 3:7 are documentary; (e) the ANE-comparative material (HL §195, MAL §41, CH §157) is documented in Roth 1995 and Westbrook 1988; (f) the step-mother-taboo at Lev 18:8, 20:11, Deut 22:30 is HB-internal-explicit; (g) the modern critical succession-claim reading is mainstream (Sarna, Westermann, Hamilton, Speiser, Alter, Westbrook, Tigay).

terms.partOfSpeech: pronominal-identification refrain (*hu Edom* = *he is Edom*; *avi Edom* = *father of Edom*)
terms.literal: he is Edom (vv 1, 8, 19) / father of Edom (vv 9, 43)
terms.standardEnglish: the same is Edom (ASV vv 1, 8, 19); Esau the father of Edom (ASV vv 9, 43); ... is Edom (NJPS / NRSV)
terms.wohChoice: the same is Edom (vv 1, 8, 19); the father of Edom (vv 9, 43) — ASV-baseline preserved; the fourfold-refrain structural significance surfaced in commentary
terms.rationale:
**The Esav-toledot block of Gen 36 is bracketed by a fourfold *hu Edom* / *avi Edom* identification-refrain at vv 1, 8, 19, and 43 (and a related variant at v 9). The refrain is editorially-load-bearing — it asserts the Esav=Edom identification four times in 43 verses — and is structurally distinct from the Gen 25:25/30 birth-and-stew etymology (which is covered by the central-glossary `esau-edom-name-etymology-double-play` entry).**

**The refrain's distribution.**
- **v 1**: *v-eleh toledot Esav hu Edom* — *and these are the generations of Esav (the same is Edom)*. The opening toledot-formula closes with the identification.
- **v 8**: *va-yeshev Esav b-har Se'ir Esav hu Edom* — *and Esav dwelt in Mount Se'ir: Esav is Edom*. The Esav-Se'ir-Edom triple-equation closes the introductory geographical-relocation section.
- **v 9**: *v-eleh toledot Esav avi Edom b-har Se'ir* — *and these are the generations of Esav the father of Edom in Mount Se'ir*. The second toledot-formula (which opens the Esav-genealogy proper) uses the variant *avi Edom* (father of Edom).
- **v 19**: *eleh b-nei Esav v-eleh alufeihem hu Edom* — *these are the sons of Esav, and these are their chiefs: the same is Edom*. The first *alufim*-list closes with the identification.
- **v 43**: *eleh alufei Edom l-moshvotam b-eretz achuzatam hu Esav avi Edom* — *these are the chiefs of Edom, according to their dwelling-places in the land of their possession. This is Esav, the father of Edom*. The chapter's closing-verse delivers the fullest form: *hu Esav avi Edom*.

**The structural function.** The fourfold refrain marks the chapter's structural-blocks:
- vv 1-8 (introduction + relocation to Se'ir): closed by v 8 *Esav hu Edom*;
- vv 9-19 (Esav's sons + first *alufim*-list): closed by v 19 *hu Edom*;
- vv 20-30 (Horite genealogy of Se'ir): no Edom-refrain (the Horite-section is structurally-separate);
- vv 31-39 (eight-kings-list): no Edom-refrain (the king-list is structurally-separate);
- vv 40-43 (second *alufim*-list): closed by v 43 *hu Esav avi Edom*.

The refrain's four occurrences therefore mark the close of each Esav-block within the chapter — the Horite (vv 20-30) and the king-list (vv 31-39) blocks are not closed with the refrain because they are not Esav-blocks. The pattern is editorially-deliberate.

**Modern critical scholarship on the refrain.** **Skinner** *ICC Genesis* 1910 pp. 430-434 reads the refrain as a P-source editorial marker, indicating that the chapter is compiled from at least two distinct genealogical sources (the *bnei Esav* + *alufei bnei Esav* material and the *bnei Se'ir ha-Chori* material) joined by the *hu Edom* identification-refrain. **Westermann** *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 559-563 treats the refrain as the chapter's P-redactional unifying-device, asserting the Esav=Edom equation against potential reader-confusion. **Hamilton** *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 388-405 reads the refrain as a redactional bracketing-device that closes each Esav-block and integrates the chapter into the larger toledot-structure of Genesis. **Friedman** *The Bible with Sources Revealed* 2003 assigns the refrain to P. **Sarna** *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 247-253 reads the refrain as preserving an old tribal-identification tradition.

**Distinct from the Gen 25 birth-etymology.** The central-glossary `esau-edom-name-etymology-double-play` entry covers the Gen 25:25/30 birth-etymology (*admoni* at birth → *adom* at the stew → *Edom*) and the *sear* → *Seir* paronomasia. The Gen 36 refrain is structurally-distinct: it is a *toledot*-structural identification-refrain, not an etymology. The two entries cover separable phenomena.

**Cross-corpus Edom-tradition reach.** The Esav=Edom equation that the refrain asserts is the foundation for the entire HB Edom-tradition: Num 20:14-21 (the *achikha Edom* — *your brother Edom* — formula in the wilderness-itinerary); Deut 2:4-8 (*echeikhem b-nei Esav* — *your brothers the sons of Esav*); Deut 23:8 [MT 23:9] (*lo t-ta'ev Adomi ki achikha hu* — *do not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother*); Obadiah (the entire short prophetic book is an Edom-judgment-oracle); Mal 1:2-5 (the *Ya'aqov ahavti v-et Esav saneti* — *Ya'aqov I loved but Esav I hated* — oracle); Ps 137:7 (the *zekhor YHWH livnei Edom* — *remember YHWH against the children of Edom* — exilic curse); Lam 4:21-22 (Edom-rejoices-at-Jerusalem's-fall lament); Ezek 25:12-14, 35:1-15 (Edom-judgment-oracles); Joel 4:19 [MT 4:19] (Edom-as-desolation). The Esav=Edom identification preserved by the Gen 36 fourfold-refrain is editorially-foundational for the entire HB Edom-Israel-relationship tradition.

**Why overlay, not central.** The fourfold-refrain is a chapter-singular structural observation — it operates within Gen 36 specifically as a redactional bracketing-device. The lexeme *Edom* itself, and the Esav=Edom equation, are covered by the central-glossary `esau-edom-name-etymology-double-play` entry (which is anchored at Gen 25 and treats the etymology). This overlay entry covers only the chapter-36-specific structural-refrain phenomenon, leaving the central entry's integrity intact.

**Modern scholarly literature.** Skinner *ICC Genesis* 1910 pp. 430-434; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 559-563; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 388-405; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 247-253; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* 1994 pp. 336-340; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 pp. 280-284; Friedman *The Bible with Sources Revealed* 2003 pp. 96-97; Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 203-205; Bartlett *Edom and the Edomites* JSOTSup 77 (1989). The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the fourfold-refrain is HB-internal-explicit at vv 1, 8, 19, 43 (with the v 9 variant *avi Edom*); (b) the structural-function as a redactional bracketing-device is mainstream modern critical scholarship; (c) the distinct-from-Gen-25 birth-etymology is documentary (the refrain is identification, not etymology); (d) the cross-corpus Edom-tradition reach is HB-internal-explicit.

terms.rationale:
**Gen 36:2-3 is the third of three HB attestations of Esav's wife-list, and the three attestations do not match cleanly. The discrepancy is one of the chapter's most-discussed editorial-critical questions, and the chapter-36 side of the doublet introduces material — specifically the placement of Oholivamah within the Anah-Tziv'on Horite-Se'irite lineage — that does not appear in the chapter-26 or chapter-28 sides. This overlay entry is the sibling of the existing central-glossary `morat-ruach-bitterness-of-spirit-esau-hittite-wives` entry, which is anchored at Gen 26:34-35 + Gen 27:46 and covers the chapter-26 side.**

**The three wife-list attestations.**

- **Gen 26:34** (J or late-P; the *morat-ruach* narrative-setup for Gen 27): *Yehudit bat-Be'eri ha-Chitti* + *Basemat bat-Elon ha-Chitti*. Two Chitti (Hittite) wives, named at the close of Gen 26 immediately before the Yitzchaq-deathbed-blessing-deception narrative of Gen 27.
- **Gen 28:9** (a later editorial bridge): + *Machalat bat-Yishma'el achot Nevayot*. After Esav perceives that the Canaanite wives are displeasing to his parents (Gen 28:8), he adds a third wife from the Yishma'elite line.
- **Gen 36:2-3** (P; the Esav-Edom genealogy): *Adah bat-Elon ha-Chitti* + *Oholivamah bat-Anah bat-Tziv'on ha-Chivvi* + *Basemat bat-Yishma'el achot Nevayot*.

**The discrepancies.**

*(a) Given-name discrepancies.* 
- The wife named *Basemat bat-Elon ha-Chitti* at Gen 26:34 is named *Adah bat-Elon ha-Chitti* at Gen 36:2 (same patronymic, different given-name).
- The wife named *Machalat bat-Yishma'el achot Nevayot* at Gen 28:9 is named *Basemat bat-Yishma'el achot Nevayot* at Gen 36:3 (same patronymic and clan-relation, different given-name).
- The wife named *Yehudit bat-Be'eri ha-Chitti* at Gen 26:34 has no clear counterpart at Gen 36:2-3 (her possible counterpart is *Oholivamah bat-Anah bat-Tziv'on ha-Chivvi*, but the patronymic and ethnonym differ).

*(b) Ethnonym discrepancies.*
- Gen 26:34 names both Esavite wives as *ha-Chitti* (Hittite).
- Gen 36:2 names Adah as *bat-Elon ha-Chitti* (the same as Basemat-of-26:34) but names Oholivamah's grandfather Tziv'on as *ha-Chivvi* (Hivite). The Gen 34:2 Shechem-Chivvi (Hivite) identification is the precedent. The MT *ha-Chivvi* at Gen 36:2 conflicts with Gen 36:20 where the same Tziv'on appears as a son of Se'ir *ha-Chori* (the Horite). The LXX and SamP at Gen 36:2 read *ha-Chori* (correcting to match v 20). The Chivvi-vs-Chori variant is covered by the central-glossary `chorim-horites-hurrian-or-cave-dweller-identification` entry.

*(c) The Oholivamah-as-Horite move.* The most-distinctive Gen 36-side feature is the placement of Oholivamah within the Anah-Tziv'on Horite-Se'irite lineage. At v 2 Oholivamah is *bat-Anah bat-Tziv'on*. At v 24 Anah is identified as the son of Tziv'on who found the *yemim* in the wilderness while pasturing his father's donkeys (covered by the central-glossary `yemim-hapax-hot-springs-mules-demons-lens-discipline` entry). At v 25 Anah's children include Dishon and *Oholivamah bat-Anah*. The chapter's internal-genealogy therefore places Oholivamah at the seam between the displacing-Esavite line and the displaced-Horite line. The Gen 36-side editorial-move integrates the Esavite lineage with the autochthonous-Horite population through Oholivamah's marriage to Esav. This integration-move does not appear in Gen 26:34 or Gen 28:9 and is structurally-significant for the chapter's ethnographic-program.

**The harmonizing-vs-source-critical readings.**

*Harmonizing-rabbinic.* The traditional rabbinic reading identifies the differently-named wives as the same persons under different names: Basemat (Gen 26:34) = Adah (Gen 36:2); Machalat (Gen 28:9) = Basemat (Gen 36:3); Yehudit (Gen 26:34) = Oholivamah (Gen 36:2). The harmonization is preserved in **Genesis Rabbah 65:2** (giving alternate-name explanations for each) and **Rashi** at Gen 36:2 (reproducing the harmonization). The reading treats the wives as bearing multiple names — a common ANE pattern (cf. Bat-Sheva / Bat-Shu'a; Yedidyah / Shlomo; etc.).

*Source-critical-modern.* The modern critical reading treats the three lists as drawn from distinct sources or traditions: **Wellhausen** *Prolegomena* 1885 / *Composition des Hexateuchs* 1899; **Skinner** *ICC Genesis* 1910 pp. 425-426 + pp. 430-434; **Eissfeldt** *Hexateuch-Synopse* 1922; **Westermann** *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 427-428 + pp. 558-560; **Friedman** *Who Wrote the Bible?* 1987 + *The Bible with Sources Revealed* 2003 (assigning Gen 26:34-35 to J or a J-supplement, Gen 28:9 to a redactional bridge, and Gen 36 to P or late-P); **Speiser** *AB Genesis* 1964 pp. 202, 280-281; **Sarna** *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 186-187 + p. 248. The source-critical reading takes the three lists as preserving distinct genealogical traditions about Esav's wives, which the final redactor preserved without smoothing-to-harmony.

**The Gen 36-side specifically.** The chapter-26 entry (`morat-ruach-bitterness-of-spirit-esau-hittite-wives`) treats the Gen 26:34-35 narrative-setup function (the wives' effect on Yitzchaq and Rivkah, the Gen 27:46 dialogue-quotation back-link) and surveys the three-list-inconsistency at a general level. The Gen 36-side specifically requires its own entry because:
*(i)* the Oholivamah-into-Horite-lineage integration is a chapter-36-specific editorial-move with consequences for the chapter's ethnographic program;
*(ii)* the chapter-36 list is the genealogical-anchor for the entire Esav-Edom toledot (the wives' children are the eponyms of the Edomite tribes);
*(iii)* the Chivvi-vs-Chori-vs-Chitti ethnonym-question is chapter-36-specific (Gen 26:34 has only Chitti; Gen 36:2 introduces Chivvi);
*(iv)* the Adah-Basemat-Oholivamah three-wife structure (vs the Gen 26 two-wife and the Gen 28 three-wife with different names) is chapter-36-specific.

**Why overlay, not central, and why a sibling rather than an appliesTo-extension.** The central-glossary `morat-ruach-bitterness-of-spirit-esau-hittite-wives` entry is anchored at Gen 26:34-35 + Gen 27:46 and is framed around the chapter-26 narrative-setup function. Extending its appliesTo to Gen 36:2-3 would conflate the chapter-26 *morat-ruach* function with the chapter-36 genealogical-anchor function, which are structurally-distinct phenomena. The ratified sibling-overlay-entries pattern (Gen 35 yisrael-second-renaming-beit-el-p-doublet as sibling of the central yisrael-name-aetiology-sarah-im-elohim entry) applies: when a load-bearing item appears in multiple chapters with different framing, create sibling entries with cross-references rather than collapsing them into a single entry.

**Modern scholarly literature.** Wellhausen *Prolegomena* 1885 / *Composition des Hexateuchs* 1899; Skinner *ICC Genesis* 1910 pp. 425-426, 430-434; Eissfeldt *Hexateuch-Synopse* 1922; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 427-428, 558-560; Friedman *Who Wrote the Bible?* 1987 and *The Bible with Sources Revealed* 2003; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 pp. 202, 280-281; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 186-187, 248; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 200-201, 390-394; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* 1994 pp. 192-193, 336-337; Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 203; Bartlett *Edom and the Edomites* JSOTSup 77 (1989); Genesis Rabbah 65:2 (harmonizing tradition); Rashi at Gen 36:2 (harmonizing tradition); HALOT s.v. the relevant proper nouns. The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the three-list discrepancy is documentary and HB-internal-explicit; (b) the source-critical reading is the mainstream modern position; (c) the harmonizing-rabbinic reading is the traditional Jewish exegetical position; (d) the Oholivamah-into-Horite-lineage integration is HB-internal-explicit through the v 2 / v 24 / v 25 chain; (e) the Chivvi-vs-Chori-vs-Chitti ethnonym question is documentary.

terms.literal: Bela son of Be'or / Bil'am son of Be'or
terms.standardEnglish: Bela the son of Beor (Gen 36:32, ASV); Balaam the son of Beor (Num 22:5, ASV)
terms.wohChoice: Bela the son of Be'or (Gen 36:32, ASV-baseline with WoH transliteration); cross-reference to Bil'am ben-Be'or of Num 22-24 surfaced in commentary
terms.rationale:
**The first Edomite king listed at Gen 36:32 is *Bela ben-Be'or* (בֶּלַע בֶּן־בְּעוֹר). The seer-prophet of the Num 22-24 narrative (and a substantial cross-corpus tradition) is *Bil'am ben-Be'or* (בִּלְעָם בֶּן־בְּעוֹר). The patronymic *ben-Be'or* is identical; the personal-names *Bela* (בֶּלַע) and *Bil'am* (בִּלְעָם) differ by a single mem-suffix and may share a Semitic root *b-l-ʿ* (*swallow*). The relationship between the two figures — name-doublet, same-figure-under-two-names, distinct-figures-sharing-a-name, or something else — is unresolved.**

**The pre-modern rabbinic identifying-tradition.** The rabbinic tradition identifies the Gen 36:32 Bela with the Num 22-24 Bil'am:
- **b. Sanhedrin 105a** — discusses Bil'am as identical with Bela ben-Be'or of Edom; the discussion includes the question whether Bil'am-as-Bela had a portion in the world-to-come (the standard rabbinic litmus-test for grave-sinners).
- **Targum Pseudo-Jonathan** at Gen 36:32 — explicitly identifies Bela with Bil'am.
- **Genesis Rabbah 82:14** — preserves the identifying-tradition.
- **Rashi** at Gen 36:32 — reproduces the identifying-tradition: *hu Bil'am ben-Be'or* (*this is Bil'am ben-Be'or*).

The rabbinic identification has interpretive consequences: Bil'am's role in Num 22-24 (a non-Israelite seer-prophet hired by Balaq king of Mo'av to curse Israel; ultimately blessing Israel under YHWH-compulsion) becomes pre-history for the Edomite-king-list, integrating the Bil'am-tradition into the broader Edomite-political-history.

**The modern critical distinguishing-tradition.** The modern critical default treats Bela and Bil'am as separate figures with a possible shared lineage or a shared regional-onomastic tradition:
- **Westermann** *Genesis 12-36* 1985 p. 567 — treats the names as distinct; the same patronymic does not require same-figure identification.
- **Hamilton** *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 402 — distinguishes the figures; treats the Gen 36:32 Bela as a real Edomite king and the Num 22 Bil'am as the Aramaean / Trans-Jordanian seer-prophet of a separate tradition.
- **Bartlett** *Edom and the Edomites* JSOTSup 77 (1989) pp. 89-90 — treats Bela as a historical Edomite king; the Bil'am-tradition is a separate Trans-Jordanian seer-tradition with a possible shared onomastic-substrate.
- **Speiser** *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 283 — distinguishes the figures.
- **Levine** *Numbers 21-36* AB 2000 pp. 137-156 — extended discussion; treats Num 22's Bil'am as the original-figure of the Trans-Jordanian seer-tradition (independent of the Edomite-king-list).
- **Sarna** *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 253 — distinguishes the figures.

**The Deir 'Alla inscription (8th c BCE).** A critical ANE-comparative anchor: the Deir 'Alla plaster-inscription, discovered in 1967 at Tell Deir 'Alla in the Jordan Valley, names *Bal'am bar-Be'or* (Aramaic *bal'am br b'r*) as a *chozeh elahin* — a *seer of the gods* — and preserves a substantial visionary-oracle attributed to him. The inscription is dated to the late-9th or 8th century BCE on paleographic and stratigraphic grounds. The standard editions and discussion:
- **Hoftijzer & van der Kooij** *Aramaic Texts from Deir 'Alla* 1976 — the foundational edition.
- **Hoftijzer & van der Kooij** eds. *The Balaam Text from Deir 'Alla Re-evaluated: Proceedings of the International Symposium Held at Leiden, 21-24 August 1989* (1991) — the follow-up symposium volume with multiple reanalyses.
- **Levine** *Numbers 21-36* AB 2000 pp. 241-275 — extensive treatment incorporating Deir 'Alla into the Bil'am-tradition reconstruction.
- **Weippert** in *The World of the Aramaeans* II (2001).

The inscription's significance: (a) it confirms the historical-existence of a *Bil'am bar-Be'or* tradition in the Trans-Jordanian region in the early Iron Age, independent of the HB; (b) it supports the modern critical reading that Bil'am of Num 22-24 is rooted in a real Trans-Jordanian seer-tradition rather than being a wholly HB-internal-literary creation; (c) it allows the possibility that the Gen 36:32 Bela ben-Be'or and the Num 22-24 Bil'am ben-Be'or represent two distinct figures sharing a regional onomastic-tradition (the patronymic *ben-Be'or* may have been a common name-formula in the region).

**The Num 22-24 cross-corpus reach.** The Bil'am-tradition has substantial cross-corpus distribution: Num 22-24 (the cursing-Israel cycle); Num 31:8, 16 (Bil'am's death in the war against Midyan; his role in the Pe'or-apostasy); Deut 23:5-6 (the prohibition on Ammonites and Moabites because of the Bil'am-hiring); Josh 13:22 (the death-of-Bil'am notice); Josh 24:9-10 (the Bil'am-cursing-blessing summary); Mic 6:5 (the Bil'am-Balaq cycle recalled in prophetic-judgment); Neh 13:2 (the Bil'am-cursing remembered in the post-exilic foreign-marriage controversy); 2 Pet 2:15-16 (Bil'am as proverbial false-prophet); Rev 2:14 (the Bil'am-trap reference).

**Why overlay, not central, and why a chapter-36 anchor.** The Bil'am-tradition's primary anchor is Num 22-24, which is outside the Genesis-WoH translation scope. Promotion of this entry to the central glossary should follow a future Num 22-Bil'am translation that has the Bil'am-narrative as its primary subject; at that point the entry's appliesTo would expand to include the Num 22-24 anchor-verses, and the entry would move to central. For now, the entry is housed in the overlay as a chapter-36-anchored cross-reference flag, documenting the rabbinic-identifying / modern-critical-distinguishing positions and the Deir 'Alla ANE-comparative anchor.
